children: At the ICC Global Business Summit, experts said water stress is already disrupting industrial activity, agriculture and livelihoods, with businesses needing to embed water resilience into investment, infrastructure and operational decisions

Water is increasingly emerging as a business continuity and economic growth risk, as climate change, groundwater depletion, rising demand and erratic rainfall put pressure on India’s limited water resources, experts said at the ICC Global Business Summit in New Delhi. The discussion brought water security into the broader conversation around economic resilience, examining its implications for industrial production, agriculture, livelihoods, infrastructure, public health and investment. The economic exposure is significant.
According to the World Bank’s 2026 assessment, water-dependent sectors contribute roughly half of India’s economic value added and employ nearly 70 per cent of its workforce.

India accounts for 18 per cent of the global population but has only 4 per cent of the world’s water resources. Around 600 million people face water stress, while increasing urbanisation, industrial demand, and climate variability are putting pressure on already constrained supplies. Aankur Patni, Chairman, ICC National Expert Committee on Water and Vice Chairman, Ion Exchange (India), said water can no longer be treated primarily as an environmental or social-development issue.

Patni also pointed to the need for public-private partnerships and commercially viable models to strengthen water security, saying the scale of the challenge would require capital, technology, and operational expertise alongside public investment.

The business impact is already visible in water-intensive industries, according to Subramaniam Varadarajan, Whole-Time Director & Chief Growth Officer, VA Tech WABAG. “We see a lot of industries not able to produce, even oil and gas kind of industries or steel or whichever industry. They have to shut down their factories for several months because they don’t have water,” Varadarajan said.

Such disruptions underline why water risk is moving closer to the core of corporate risk management. A shortage can translate into production losses, higher water-treatment costs, delayed expansion, supply-chain disruption, and greater dependence on alternative sources.

The issue also extends beyond individual industrial sites. Water-intensive sectors are interconnected through the water-energy-food-environment nexus. The Global Commission on the Economics of Water has highlighted how disruption in one system can create knock-on effects across others, including impacts on agricultural output, energy generation and food-processing systems.

For India, agriculture remains particularly important to this equation. The World Bank estimates that agriculture uses 80–90 per cent of the country’s water, and increasing reliance on groundwater has depleted aquifers in several areas. This makes water resilience relevant not only for farmers and utilities but also for companies exposed to agricultural commodities, food processing, consumer goods and rural markets.

Vibha Dhawan, Director General, The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) and Chancellor, TERI School of Advanced Studies, stressed the wider development implications of water investment. “Investment in water means that we are also investing in all of the sustainable development goals,” Dhawan said. Her observation reflects the wider economic multiplier associated with water infrastructure. Reliable water services can improve productivity, reduce time spent securing water, support livelihoods and strengthen public health, while better resource management can improve resilience against climate-related shocks.
From Water Infrastructure To Water Economics

The discussion also highlighted the need to change the way water is valued and managed. William Rex, World Bank Practice Manager and Head of Water Practice for India, World Bank Group, said India’s fundamental constraint is not simply the quantity of water available but how effectively it is managed.

“India is never going to have more than 4 per cent of the world’s water. The challenge is management. It’s more and more sophisticated ways to manage water cooperatively,” Rex said. The World Bank estimates that India’s urban water infrastructure alone will require around USD 150 billion over the next 15 years, alongside investment in storage, irrigation and flood management. It has also argued for stronger financial models that can attract commercial capital into water services.

The financing question is becoming increasingly relevant as cities and industries face a combination of ageing infrastructure, water losses, rising demand and more frequent climate extremes. Fredrick Royan, Associate Partner & Global Practice Area Leader, Sustainability and Circular Economy, Frost & Sullivan and Co-Chair, SWAN India Alliance, highlighted the economy-wide nature of the challenge, with consequences extending across agriculture, rural livelihoods, urban development, industry, investment and public health.

The panel also featured Ashish Pandey, Head, Centre for Sustainable Rural Development (CSRD), IIT Roorkee, and Dr Nitin Bassi, Fellow and Lead, Sustainable Water, Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), bringing academic and research perspectives to the discussion. For corporate India, the emerging message is that water risk will increasingly need to sit alongside other enterprise risks such as energy security, climate exposure and supply-chain resilience. Companies could increasingly need to assess water availability when making decisions on industrial site selection, capital expenditure, insurance, supply-chain planning, climate-risk assessment and expansion into water-stressed regions.

The transition also opens a larger opportunity for the water economy, from wastewater treatment and recycling to desalination, water-efficiency technologies, digital monitoring, leakage reduction and resource recovery. As the World Bank notes, water-dependent sectors are central to India's jobs and economic activity. The challenge, therefore, is no longer simply how to secure water for communities or industries, but how to build an economy that can continue to function as water availability becomes increasingly uncertain. As India pursues higher manufacturing capacity, urbanisation, and infrastructure expansion, water security is increasingly becoming part of the country's economic resilience equation.
